## Where the idea comes from {.smaller .deepdive run="multiverse"}

::: {.skiplink}
[Multiverse tutorial, 8 slides – skip to the class chart →](#the-class-multiverse)
:::

::: {.small}
- **Multiverse analysis** [@SteegenEtAl2016IncreasingTransparencyMultiverse] – developed for *data-processing* choices: how you code, exclude and combine. Report the whole set of datasets that your choices could have produced
- **Specification curve analysis** [@SimonsohnEtAl2020SpecificationCurveAnalysis] – the same move for *model* choices, plus a visual grammar: estimates on top, the choices that produced each one underneath
- **The vibration of effects** – the same idea, arrived at independently in epidemiology
- **The book-length treatment** [@YoungCumberworth2025MultiverseAnalysisComputational] – computational recipes at scale
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Under all these names the proposal is the same: **stop treating your analytical choices as invisible, and enumerate them.**
:::

::: notes
The vocabulary of this field is confused, so I take the terms in the order in which they arrived. Multiverse analysis comes from Steegen and colleagues in 2016 and grew out of the choices of data processing, how a variable is coded, which cases are excluded and how items are combined, with the proposal to report the whole set of datasets that those choices could have produced. Specification curve analysis, by Simonsohn, Simmons and Nelson, makes the same move for the choices of the model and adds a display, with the estimates on top and, beneath them, a panel of the choices that produced each one. The vibration of effects is the same idea, arrived at independently in epidemiology, and there is now a book-length treatment with computational recipes. [advance] Under all these names the proposal is to stop treating analytical choices as invisible and to enumerate them.
:::

## The garden of forking paths {#the-garden-drawn .smaller .deepdive run="multiverse"}

```{r}
#| label: forking-paths
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.6
# A binary decision tree over four choices: 16 end points, one path highlighted.
# Drawn from coordinates rather than data – this is an illustration of the
# structure of a decision sequence, not a result.
lev <- 4
seg <- purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(lev), \(k) {
  n_parent <- 2^(k - 1)
  purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(n_parent), \(j) {
    y0 <- (j - 0.5) / n_parent
    tibble::tibble(
      x = k - 1, xend = k,
      y = y0,
      yend = c(y0 - 0.5 / 2^k, y0 + 0.5 / 2^k),
      lit = k <= 1 | FALSE)
  })
})
# Highlight one route through the tree: always the upper branch.
route <- tibble::tibble(x = 0:3, xend = 1:4,
                        y = c(0.5, 0.75, 0.875, 0.9375),
                        yend = c(0.75, 0.875, 0.9375, 0.96875))

ggplot2::ggplot() +
  ggplot2::geom_segment(data = seg, ggplot2::aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
               colour = "#c7ccd2", linewidth = 0.5) +
  ggplot2::geom_segment(data = route, ggplot2::aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
               colour = d_red, linewidth = 1.1) +
  ggplot2::annotate("text", x = 0:3 + 0.5, y = -0.06,
           label = c("outcome", "estimator", "sample", "weights"),
           colour = ncl_blue, fontface = "bold", size = 4.2) +
  ggplot2::annotate("text", x = 4.05, y = 0.96875, hjust = 0,
           label = "the one you published",
           colour = d_red, fontface = "bold", size = 4.2) +
  ggplot2::coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 5.6), ylim = c(-0.1, 1.05), clip = "off") +
  ggplot2::theme_void()
```

::: {.small}
Four binary choices give sixteen analyses. **Fourteen decisions with several options each give more than a million.** The published paper reports one red line and no tree.
:::

::: notes
The chart draws the structure of the problem. Four choices with two options each already give sixteen distinct analyses, and our menu has fourteen decisions, more than half of them with more than two options, which takes us from sixteen to more than a million. The red line is what a published paper reports, one route through the tree with no indication that the tree exists. The reader receives a coefficient and a standard error, and the standard error describes the uncertainty of sampling, with no information about the fifteen other branches. Gelman and Loken call this the garden of forking paths, and their observation, which we met earlier, is that no one has to walk every path for the problem to arise, since walking one path chosen after looking at the data is enough.
:::

## Filters for inclusion {#justifiable-not-merely-possible .smaller .deepdive run="multiverse"}

::: {.small}
Two filters decide which of the analyses you could run go into a multiverse:

- **Justifiability** – could you defend this specification to a reviewer, in writing, before seeing its result?
- **The same estimand** – does it estimate the quantity you said you were after?
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Drop the first filter and you get a cloud of nonsense that makes any finding look fragile. Drop the second and you are averaging over answers to different questions – which is the red-card mistake, at scale.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Our curve is a **curated `r format(nrow(spec_curve), big.mark = ",")`**: a review put both filters to every option of the menu, and the [decision map]({{< var site-url >}}menu.html#map) gives the reason for each option left off. That curation is itself an analytical decision, and it is the one that a critic should attack first.
:::

::: notes
Multiverse analysis is most often done badly at this point. A multiverse is not every analysis that one could run, because two filters have to be passed before a specification goes in. The first is justifiability, whether you could defend the specification to a reviewer, in writing, before knowing its result, and the second is that it estimates the quantity that you said you were after. [advance] Drop the first filter and you obtain a cloud of nonsense, which scatters the answers so that any finding looks fragile. Drop the second, and you average over answers to different questions, which is the mistake of the red-card study reproduced at scale. [advance] Our curve is a curated set of eight hundred and sixty-four, in which every option of the menu was reviewed against both filters, and the decision map gives the reason for each option left off. The curation is itself an analytical decision, and the first that a critic should attack, which is why its reasons are published beside the curve.
:::

## Enumeration and curation {#enumerate-or-curate .smaller .deepdive run="multiverse"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**Enumerate**

Cross every option on every axis. Complete, mechanical, reproducible.

Risk: the set fills up with specifications that nobody would defend, and the spread stops meaning anything.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**Curate**

Include only the specifications you would actually defend.

Risk: you are choosing the set, so a sceptic can ask whether you chose it to get the picture you wanted.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .small}
Either way, **the set is a claim**, and it belongs in the paper alongside the curve, ideally preregistered before the curve is drawn.
:::

::: notes
There are two strategies for building the set, and both have a real cost. To enumerate is to cross every option on every axis mechanically, which is complete and reproducible and protects you from the charge of hand-picking, but the set then fills with specifications that nobody would defend, and once it does, the spread stops meaning anything, since analyses that are wrong were included. To curate is to include only the specifications that you would defend in print, which solves the first problem and creates a second, because you now choose the set, and a sceptic can reasonably ask whether you chose it to produce the picture that you wanted. I do not think that this dilemma can be escaped. [advance] Either way the set is a claim, which belongs in the paper beside the curve and is ideally preregistered before the curve is drawn.
:::

## Multiplying the menu out {#the-arithmetic-gets-away-from-you .smaller .deepdive run="multiverse"}

::: {.small}
Our menu, multiplied out:

- The curve: 3 positive scales × (4 unemployment series × 2 forms + 1 growth series) × 2 adjustments × 2 estimators × 2 no-opinion rules × 2 item sets × 2 cell weightings → **`r format(nrow(spec_curve), big.mark = ",")`**
- The full menu: every option of the thirteen decisions that change an estimate, before the admissibility rules remove the combinations that do not exist → **`r format(n_full_menu, big.mark = ",")`**, each of which can be tested in five ways
- Open the **unit of analysis** as well – person level or aggregate – and the arithmetic doubles again
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Two consequences. **Compute stops being free**, so somebody must decide what is worth running. And **nobody can read that many numbers** – you need a picture, a way to ask which decision is doing the work, and reasons for leaving options out.
:::

::: notes
The curve comes first: three positive scales, nine ways of measuring the economy, four unemployment series in two forms and growth, two adjustment sets, two estimators, and two options on each of the three measurement decisions that the review kept, which gives eight hundred and sixty-four. The full menu, every option of every decision that changes an estimate, before the rules of admissibility remove the combinations that do not exist, gives about one point seven million, each of which could be tested in five ways, and opening the unit of analysis as well, person or aggregate, would double the number again. [advance] Two consequences follow. Computing stops being free, so somebody has to decide what is worth running, a decision that is not neutral. And nobody can read that many numbers, so you need a picture, a way of asking which decision is doing the work, and written reasons for every option that you leave out.
:::

## Purposes of a multiverse {#what-is-a-multiverse-for .smaller .deepdive run="multiverse"}

::: {.small}
Rohrer, Hullman and Gelman's question, and it has three different answers that need three differently built universes:

- **Reflection** – to understand your own analysis. Which choices matter, where the argument has to happen. Build it broad, and read it yourself
- **Persuasion** – to convince a reader that the finding is not an artefact of one path. Build it from specifications that *your critic* would accept
- **Inference** – to make a probabilistic statement about the curve as a whole. Build it to a rule fixed in a preregistration, and bring a null distribution
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The full menu, with the decision map, serves **reflection**. The curve keeps only what a review judged justifiable for this claim, which moves it towards **persuasion**. Reading either as inference is a mistake that we take apart later.
:::

::: {.src}
@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood
:::

::: notes
The question that organises the debate is the one asked by Rohrer, Hullman and Gelman, what a multiverse is for, and its three answers need three differently built sets. For reflection, to understand your own analysis, which choices matter and where the argument has to take place, you build the set broad and read it yourself, and it need not go into the paper at all. For persuasion, to convince a reader that the finding is not an artefact of one path, you build it from specifications that your critic would accept. For inference, a probabilistic statement about the curve as a whole, you need a rule fixed in a preregistration and a null distribution, a much heavier undertaking. [advance] In this workshop the full menu, with the decision map, serves reflection, and the curve keeps only the options judged justifiable for this claim, which moves it towards persuasion, since a critic can check each reason. Reading either as inference is a mistake that we take apart later.
:::

## Decomposing the variance by fork {#which-fork-matters .smaller .deepdive run="multiverse"}

::: {.small}
Once you have hundreds of estimates and the choices that produced each one, you can ask a question that no single analysis can answer: **how much of the variation does each axis account for?**

- Treat the curve as data: one row per specification, the decisions as factors, the estimate as the outcome
- Decompose the variance across decisions
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The answer is the most useful thing that a multiverse produces, because it tells you **where to spend your argument**. An axis that moves nothing does not need defending, while an axis that moves everything needs a paragraph.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
On this claim, the answer surprises almost everybody who guesses it in advance.
:::

::: notes
This analysis becomes possible only once there are hundreds of estimates and a record of the choices that produced each one. The curve itself becomes a dataset, with one row per specification, the nine decisions that vary on it as factors and the estimate as the outcome, and the variance is decomposed across decisions. [advance] I think that this decomposition is the most useful product of a multiverse, more useful than the curve itself, because it tells you where to spend your argument: an axis that moves nothing needs a sentence in your paper, and an axis that moves everything needs a paragraph of justification and probably an analysis of sensitivity. [advance] On this claim the answer surprises nearly everybody who guesses it in advance.
:::

## Reading a specification curve {.smaller .deepdive run="multiverse"}

::: {.small}
Five questions to ask any curve you meet, in any paper:

1. **What is on the vertical axis** – a raw coefficient, or something standardised? Are the signs aligned so that up and down mean the same thing throughout?
2. **How was the set built** – enumerated or curated, and by whom?
3. **Where does the published estimate sit** – at the median, or out at an end?
4. **Is the spread patterned** – does one axis produce the extremes, or is it scattered?
5. **What test classes the points, and against what null** – are the errors clustered, and are the specifications independent? (They almost never are.)
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Answered for your own curve, the five make a publishable robustness section.
:::

::: notes
The tutorial closes with five questions to ask of any specification curve, in anybody's paper. The first is what the vertical axis shows, a raw coefficient, which is not comparable across outcomes, or something standardised, and whether the signs are aligned so that up and down mean the same thing throughout. The second is how the set was built, enumerated or curated, and by whom, and the third where the published estimate sits, at the median or at one end, two very different situations for an author. The fourth is whether the spread is patterned, with one axis producing the extremes, or scattered. The fifth, which few people ask, is which test classes the points, against what null, with or without errors that allow for clustering, and whether the specifications are independent of each other, which they almost never are. [advance] Answered for your own curve, the five questions give the material for a publishable section on robustness.
:::
